item.title: The rate-hike trade just broke, and the S&P ran straight through 7,800
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: September hike odds collapsed from 42.1 to 29 percent in one session on a hold call from Oxford Economics that said the Fed may not move for the rest of the year.
item.content:encoded:
September hike odds collapsed from 42.1 to 29 percent in one session on a hold call from Oxford Economics that said the Fed may not move for the rest of the year.

Yesterday the market still had a September hike at 42.1 percent chances after a CPI that landed on the estimate to the decimal. Today the floor fell out.

Market context. The S&P 500 broke above 7,800 for the first time ever, an intraday record, and the VIX touched 14.39, a new 2026 low. The session ran on energy: a Houthi attack on the Aramco refinery sent diesel cracks through $98 a barrel for an all-time high, gold futures held above $4,500 for the first time since June 5, and the yen inched back toward 160 per dollar. The 30-year auctioned at 5.21 percent on Tuesday and has not come in. Volume was the lowest in thirteen sessions for the S&P, which has now printed 26 all-time highs in 2026.

1. The hike odds broke, and the pivot reversed faster than it built. On Tuesday the market priced a September hike at 48.4 percent. On Wednesday it was 42.1 after the CPI. Today it is 29, and the hold stands at 70. Oxford Economics published a note saying the Fed is likely to hold for the rest of 2026, pointing to PCE inflation of 3.6 percent year over year in July against 3.7 in June and a labour market that is weakening but not breaking.

That is a fast trip. A month ago the September hike was at 69 percent. The jobs report took it to 48, the CPI nudged it to 42, and today a four-line forecast from a named shop took it to 29. The sequence is telling: a single payroll print, a single house call, and a single refinery attack have now dismantled more than 40 points of hike pricing in nine days. One more print, one more hawk to retreat, and the hold is a consensus.

The dissent is thin and it is not about the data. Warren Pies is still at a hike at 38 percent, arguing that the committee is under political pressure from a persistently missed inflation target, and he names Beth Hammack directly. Hammack herself said today that raising rates is painful but the Fed must not let growth and investment overheat. She did not say September and she did not say hold. The other hawk, Warsh, was quiet today.

What makes the pivot faster than the build is that the tail is pricing the same thing the front is. The December hike fell from 73.8 to 62.3. The October hike moved from 62.2 to 48.6. Any hike in 2026 is now at 47 percent, down from above 75 two weeks ago. When the back end of the year moves more than the front, the market is not just pricing a delay. It is pricing a reversal of the call. Goldman Sachs already declared the hold on Wednesday and nobody has stepped in front of them.

2. Iran is now asserting control over the strait and the oil market noticed. Iran said today that no vessel can transit the Strait of Hormuz without its permission. It reorganized its military to be more aggressive abroad, the State Department told embassies to draw up reduced-staff plans on fears of a return to war, and the US is sending a fresh carrier group led by the USS George Washington. The Reaper drone fleet is down about a quarter, with 45 MQ-9s lost at a replacement cost above $1.3 billion. The Pentagon is seeking $67 billion to replenish them.

The price is in diesel. Cracks broke above $98 a barrel, an all-time high, after the Houthis hit a Saudi Aramco refinery. A market that was oversupplied on paper at 106.3 million barrels a day of supply against 104.8 million of demand closed at a chokepoint it cannot control. Iran says it can keep the strait shut as long as necessary and that it is considering prolonging the war until Trump leaves office. Trump himself said the US has total control of the strait and thinks it will keep it.

Yesterday the Polymarket contract on the US announcing an end to the blockade by October 31 fell from 93 percent to 73. It has not moved back up today. The year-end contract sat at 81 cents.

3. Three firms reported after the bell and the after-hours trade is saying what the session trade already told you. Coherent beat, guided above the street, and fell six percent. Cerebras beat and fell fourteen, because operating expense came in at $500 million against $80 million expected and at a $60 billion market cap on less than a billion dollars of revenue, the valuation math matters the moment the numbers are not perfect. Cisco beat on networking products up 40 percent year over year and a Q1 guide more than a billion above the street, and still faded to red after hours.

The pattern is the same one the morning held: the S&P rallied 0.6 percent to a record and the headliners inside it, the $NVDA and the $NBIS and the semis, did the running, while the rest of the index held still. The equal-weight S&P is up fourteen of the last sixteen months. The cap-weight index is rallying because the megacaps are rallying, and the after-hours earnings are selectively punishing the ones whose numbers were not clean enough.

4. The bond market is doing its own thing and the yen is the link. The thirty-year auctioned at 5.21 percent on Tuesday, the highest in a quarter century, and the yield has barely moved from there. Japan's two-year hit 1.64 percent, the first time since 1995, while the yen pushed back toward 160 per dollar. At 160 the intervention question returns, because that is the level that triggered the first coordinated US-Japan intervention since 1998 last month alongside the Bessent FIMA repo proposal.

CreditSights published a note today saying the Fed could hold into 2027. If the long end is at 5.21 and the front end is holding, that is the steepener trade the rate-cut trade was built on. The yen at 160 and the thirty-year at 5.21 are two sides of a funding question, and the fuel on both sides is the deficit. The national debt hit a record $39.94 trillion today, this fiscal year's deficit is already larger than all of last year's, and $1.1 trillion a year in interest is the floor under the long end regardless of what the Fed does with the overnight rate.

item.title: The print landed exactly on consensus and moved September by six points
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: I said CPI would settle September more than payrolls did, and it did not come close, so that call is a miss and this is what it actually moved.
item.content:encoded:
I said CPI would settle September more than payrolls did, and it did not come close, so that call is a miss and this is what it actually moved.

Yesterday I said the thing to watch was whether the month-over-month number started with a 2. Headline started with a 1, core started with a 2, everything printed on the estimate, and September barely moved.

Market context. The print was in line on every line that was published.

July CPIActualEstimatePrior
Headline, year over year3.4 percent3.43.5
Core, year over year2.5 percent2.52.6
Core, month over month0.2 percent0.2minus 0.0
Headline, month over month0.1 percent0.1

One correction to yesterday. I printed a monthly consensus of 0.32 percent from a single source. The number the desks were actually carrying was 0.1 percent on headline and 0.2 on core, and the print matched it. The 0.32 was wrong and I should have checked it against a second source before publishing it.

Per the People to follow list, core goods rose 0.2 percent, the biggest monthly increase since September 2025. That is the one line inside the report that does not read friendly. Gold went the other way from a benign print. Per the Kalshi list, gold futures surged back above $4,500, the first time since June 5, against spot near $4,408 overnight. Per the Financial Markets list, the yen is inching toward 160 per dollar and raising re-intervention concerns, and the session ran on the lightest volume of the past thirteen trading days.

The scoreboard.

  • Miss, and cleanly. On the 6th I called the August 12 CPI the print that settles September more than payrolls does. Payrolls moved September hike odds from 55 percent to roughly 40. CPI moved them from 48.4 to 42.1. Payrolls moved it more than twice as far. Section one is the accounting.
  • Miss, and I saw it coming too late. My call that a joint Iran-Oman announcement lands inside a week expires today with no announcement. I opened it at 70/30, cut to 55/45, then to 40/60 yesterday. The direction was right at the end and the original number was not. Section two.

1. Six points is what a perfectly in-line print buys you. Per the People to follow list, the post-CPI repricing was orderly and small.

Fed hike odds, after against beforeReading
September 1642.1 percent, from 48.4
October 2856.3 percent, from 62.2
December 973.8 percent, from 78.9
Any hike in 202655 percent, from over 75 earlier this month

Per the Polymarket list, Goldman Sachs went further and declared outright that the Fed holds in September. That is the first named house call for a hold in a week of this desk carrying one.

My 60/40 for a September hold is now roughly where the market is, with a hike at 42.1 against my implied 40. Holding it is no longer a contrarian position, and saying that is more useful than claiming vindication.

The dissent is specific and it is not dovish. Per the Stocks list, Warren Pies says a September hike at 38 percent is underpriced, that he would hold but that the committee is "increasingly feeling the political pressure of persistently missing its inflation target," and that today's data is not decisive enough to offset the political dynamics. He names Beth Hammack directly.

The reason my call missed is that I confused a scheduled event with a decisive one. A print that lands on the estimate to the decimal on four separate lines cannot move a distribution much, almost by construction. Payrolls surprised by 103,000 jobs and moved it fifteen points. CPI surprised by nothing and moved it six. The lesson I am taking is that the size of a repricing comes from the surprise, not from the importance of the series, and I priced importance.

Note what did not move. December still sits at 73.8 percent for a hike. The year is not settled and today did not settle it.

2. Hormuz resolved, and it resolved against everybody who wanted a deal. No joint Iran-Oman announcement landed. What landed instead was worse.

Per the Polymarket list, Iran says there are no talks to extend the ceasefire, adds that the ceasefire never officially took effect, and accuses Washington of violating it inside 48 hours. The State Department has ordered US embassies across the Middle East to draw up contingency plans for operating with reduced staff on fears of a return to war. Per the Kalshi list, Iran is reported to be considering prolonging the war until Trump leaves office. Trump's own line today was that the US has "total control" over the Strait of Hormuz and "I think we will keep it."

The cleanest read is in a price. Per the People to follow morning list, the odds of the US announcing an end to the Iranian blockade by October 31 fell from 93 percent to 73 in a single week on $12.2 million of volume, with the cliff starting on August 8. A separate contract on the blockade being lifted by year end decayed from above 95 cents to about 81. The market spent the week pricing the deal further away, not closer.

I opened this at 70/30 for an announcement inside a week and it finished at zero. The cut to 40/60 yesterday was right and late. The error that produced the original number was treating Iran's route agreement with Oman as a proxy for the strait reopening, which Iran itself spent this week explicitly denying.

3. Gold cleared $4,500 into a benign inflation print, and that is not what it is supposed to do. Per the Kalshi list and the Financial Markets list, futures are back above $4,500 for the first time since June 5 and spot ran about 1 percent overnight to $4,408.79. Somebody keeps buying it in size, with a third unusual multi-million-dollar call print inside a week.

Against that, per the People to follow list, Cathie Wood expects a deflationary boom and gold to fall. The betting markets are not with her and not fully with gold either: traders price only a 17 percent chance Bitcoin outperforms gold in 2026, down nine points.

Gold rallying on a cooling CPI while the long end still prices three quarters odds of a December hike is the debasement trade rather than the inflation trade. Those are different arguments and only one of them cares what the print said.

4. The yen is back at 160 and that is the number that ends the quiet. Per the Financial Markets list, the yen is inching toward 160 per dollar and raising re-intervention concerns. That is the level that produced the first coordinated US-Japan intervention since 1998 last month, the one that came with the Bessent proposal to expand the Fed's FIMA repo facility so Japan could borrow dollars against Treasuries rather than sell them. Per the Financial Markets morning list, Japan's two-year yield hit 1.64 percent, the first time since 1995, and Japan is the largest foreign holder of Treasuries at roughly $1.2 trillion. The US 30-year is at its highest since 2007.

The oil side gives the yen no help. Per the Financial Markets list, the IEA revised 2025 demand up to 104.8 million barrels a day against supply of 106.3 million, US crude stockpiles posted an unexpected build, Russian output ran nearly a million barrels a day below its OPEC quota in July, and US imports of Venezuelan crude hit a nine-year high. A market that is oversupplied on paper and closed at a chokepoint in practice is one headline away from either direction.

If the yen takes 160 while Hormuz stays shut, the intervention question comes back inside weeks rather than months. That is the thing on the calendar that nobody has a date for.

item.title: Iran says the Oman deal and the strait are separate, and crude went through $90
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Tehran now wants the war ended and its funds unfrozen before the strait reopens, and I am cutting my own announcement call to 40/60 the day before it comes due.
item.content:encoded:
Tehran now wants the war ended and its funds unfrozen before the strait reopens, and I am cutting my own announcement call to 40/60 the day before it comes due.

Yesterday I cut the Hormuz call to 55/45 because Iran had started separating the Oman route from the strait itself. Today the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council said it in a sentence, and the oil market believed him.

Market context. Crude is doing the arguing. Per the Market list, oil surged 5 percent Monday as Hormuz deal hopes faded, with Brent settling at $87.72 and WTI reaching $82.13. Per the Financial Markets morning list, Brent was around $88 this morning, and per the Crypto list it then traded above $90. Gold went with it, reclaiming $4,400 for the first time since early June per the Kalshi list, where traders also price 75 percent that gold outperforms Bitcoin this year. Equities did nothing at all. Per Arbitrage Andy, the S&P finished Monday roughly unchanged near 7,753, and per the Financial Markets list today was another consolidation session with the index near its lows, waiting on tomorrow.

The scoreboard.

  • Due tomorrow, and I am cutting it below even. My call that a joint Iran-Oman announcement lands inside a week goes from 55/45 to 40/60 against. Section one is why, and this now resolves as a miss more often than not.
  • Due tomorrow. The August 12 CPI I called on the 6th as the print that settles September. Consensus is 0.32 percent month over month and 3.4 percent year over year against 3.5 prior. Section three is what it decides.

1. Iran separated the two agreements out loud, and that is the thing I got wrong twice. Per the Market list, Mohsen Rezaei said at 3:49pm that if an Iran-Oman transit agreement is reached, "this will be a separate matter from the closure of the strait." Three minutes earlier he set the price of reopening: "as long as the US does not change its behavior and accept Iran's conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened," with the war ended and Iranian funds unfrozen named specifically and other conditions passed through mediators.

My call names the announcement, not the reopening, so it is not dead. It is now a call on a document Iran has publicly stripped of consequence.

The route track is alive. Per the Polymarket list, Qatar says the Oman-Iran negotiations are at an advanced stage with positive feedback from both, and Pakistan's defence minister told Bloomberg the US and Iran are "close to some sort of arrangement."

Per CaspianReport, the sticking point is a toll. Iran wants its right to collect tolls on transit recognised and says the June agreement implied it. Washington disagrees, and that rejection triggered the worst fighting since the April ceasefire. Oman has reportedly secured Gulf Arab backing for a voluntary toll system, and the two capitals are still far apart on it. Iran absorbed the strikes without conceding, so the price of a deal went up rather than down. Trump's framing today was that Iran "agrees privately, refuses publicly."

I am cutting to 40/60 rather than closing it out, because Qatar and Pakistan both describe a document in its final stage and the date is tomorrow. Two of my last three moves here have been downward, for the same reason each time: I kept pricing the route as though it were the strait.

The physical market is where the disagreement shows. Per the morning Financial Markets list, Hormuz remains closed to LNG traffic, curtailing about 20 percent of global supply, while Trump says the strait "is open now" behind an "infallible" Navy blockade. Per Capital Flows, the MOVE index is at its lows against a resilient economy and a crude supply shock is what blows it out. Brent moved ten percent in two sessions while rate volatility sat still, and the strategic reserve is below 300 million barrels for the first time in over forty years.

2. The Fed argument is hike against hold, and almost nobody is pricing a cut. That matters because my 60/40 is a hold call, and a hold is the dovish end of the live range rather than its middle.

Where September is pricedReading
Bank of Americastill 75bp of hikes this year, first one in September
FedWatch before the payrolls miss, per Milk Road55 percent chance of a hike
FedWatch after it, per Milk Roadhold is base case at 60 percent, Kalshi 65
FedWatch before and after, per ClearValue Tax67 percent hike, then 51.7 against 48.3 no change
Atlanta Fed's Venable, today"inflation is too high"

Those readings do not agree and I will not pretend they do. One has a hold as the clear base case, another has it at a coin flip, and per VirtualBacon the September 16 meeting sits at 48 percent no hike against 51 percent hike, the most indecisive he has seen. What they agree on is direction: per the Stocks list, the payrolls miss took a hike off the table rather than putting a cut on it, and July's FOMC held 9 to 3 with three members wanting to raise.

Per the Market morning list, Bank of America is sticking with the hiking call despite payrolls falling 23,000 and prior months revised down by 103,000, because inflation remains its central concern. Per ClearValue Tax, who carries the FedWatch series, has his own money on no increase in September, bought when it was a bigger underdog than it is now. The bond market is with the hawks: per Capital Flows, the weakness is bear steepening, and a long end selling off faster than the front end says policy is not restrictive enough.

I am holding 60/40 for a hold, and I want to be precise about what it is not. It is not a call that the Fed eases. Almost nobody in today's material expects that. It is a call that a committee looking at negative payrolls does not hike into them, and two separate series have that at roughly a coin flip. VirtualBacon's cumulative number is the uncomfortable one: 80 to 85 percent odds of at least one hike by year end, which makes September a question of timing rather than direction.

3. Tomorrow's print comes with a threshold attached rather than just a forecast. Per Milk Road, consensus is 0.32 percent month over month against their own break level of 0.20, so consensus already sits above the line that flips their posture from risk-on to caution. An in-line print does it without running hot. Meanwhile July average hourly earnings grew 3.2 percent against a June CPI of 3.5, so real wages are negative while the labour market sheds jobs. The thing to watch is not the headline. It is whether the month-over-month number starts with a 2.

4. CLARITY finally has a date, and the odds that matter did not move at all. Per VirtualBacon, John Thune filed cloture on Sunday and the vote is set for 2:15pm Eastern on Tuesday September 15, once the Senate work period resumes on the 14th.

The arithmetic is why nobody is excited. Cloture needs 60, Republicans hold 53, Thune's committee counts two Democrats already on board, so the bill is about five votes short.

CLARITY, as pricedOdds
Kalshi, becomes law this year23 percent, up from 13 before the date was set
Polymarket27 percent
Galaxy Research30 percent
By October 202740 percent, against 41 before the announcement

That last line is the whole story. Scheduling a vote moved the this-year number ten points and moved the eighteen-month number down one. The market read a date as a timing detail rather than as new information about whether it passes, and given that cloture only decides whether to take the bill up, with thirty hours of debate, amendments and a likely second cloture sequence behind it, that looks right.

item.title: Iran is close on Oman and says that still does not reopen the strait
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Tehran's price is now US withdrawal, war reparations and the blockade lifted, Polymarket has a deal by month end at 30 percent, and both crude benchmarks rose a dollar on the doubt.
item.content:encoded:
Tehran's price is now US withdrawal, war reparations and the blockade lifted, Polymarket has a deal by month end at 30 percent, and both crude benchmarks rose a dollar on the doubt.

Yesterday I said the Hormuz call was the one I was least comfortable with. Tehran spent the weekend proving the discomfort was right and the number was not.

Market context. Gold is the asset doing the arguing. Per the Financial Markets list, it is easing back from a seven-week high of $4,372 while the dollar recovers from its post-payrolls slump on renewed Hormuz risk. Per the Kalshi list, Kalshi's traders forecast $4,566 this year, about 4.4 percent above that high. Crude went the other way from the headlines, with Brent and WTI each up more than a dollar. Wednesday's CPI is the only event on the calendar that matters.

The scoreboard.

  • Due Wednesday, and I am cutting it. My 70/30 that a joint Iran-Oman announcement lands inside a week goes to 55/45. Section one is the reason.
  • Due Wednesday. The August 12 CPI print I called on the 6th as the thing that settles September more than payrolls did. That still looks right, and it is now carrying more weight than I wanted it to.

1. Iran got closer to Oman and further from reopening, and those are two different agreements. Per the Market list, Iran says it is "very close to an agreement with Oman" on a new maritime transit route, and in the same breath warns that an Oman deal would not mean the strait reopens.

That distinction is the whole trade, and I underweighted it. My call was written on the route agreement being real, and the route agreement is real. It just turns out to be the cheap half.

Tehran's stated price for the strait itself is now explicit and maximal.

| Iran's preconditions to reopen Hormuz | |---| | US forces withdrawn from the region | | The naval blockade lifted | | Sanctions removed and frozen assets released | | An end to proxy warfare | | War reparations | | An end to hostile rhetoric |

Against that list, per the Polymarket list, the market prices a US-Iran Hormuz agreement by the end of the month at 30 percent, and it moved to that from a higher projection. Per the Kalshi list, Iran rejected talks outright over the weekend.

The two governments are also describing different games. Trump told Axios the US is only "semi-negotiating" and that it is "low-keying it", with oil near $75 doing the work of cushioning the consumer while the blockade grinds. Araghchi says no talks are happening at all and cannot restart while Washington breaches the June interim agreement. Pezeshkian says now is the best time for a deal. Three positions, one government on each side, and only one of them is a negotiation.

I am cutting the announcement call to 55/45 rather than killing it, because the Oman route genuinely is close and that is what the call names. What I got wrong was treating the route as a proxy for the strait. It is not, and Iran said so itself.

2. The Fed question that nobody would put a number on today. Friday's payrolls settled nothing. Per Milk Road, July shed 23,000 jobs against an expected gain of 80,000, and unemployment still fell from 4.2 percent to 4.1 because 264,000 people left the labour force. Participation is 61.4 percent, the lowest since early 2021. A print that bad on the headline and that ambiguous underneath is why nobody moved.

What did move is the framing. The Fed risk in this feed is being discussed as a hike, not a cut, with the Street reading Asian currencies as buoyed by reduced rate-hike prospects. Funds sit at 3.50 to 3.75 percent and roughly one hike is still priced for 2026.

Milk Road's mechanism for that hike never arriving is the one specific thing on offer: Kevin Warsh has five task forces running on inflation, jobs, data and the balance sheet, and the expectation is that one returns hawkish and four return dovish, which hands him the cover to cut instead.

I am holding 60/40 for a September hold, unchanged from yesterday. Not one source in today's material published a September probability, and Jordi Visser, who had it at 45 percent, wrote three thousand words on Japan without restating it. When the desks that were arguing go quiet in the same week as the print, the print is the argument. Wednesday settles it.

3. The yen rescue got its plumbing explained, and the answer is the Fed's balance sheet. Per Jordi Visser, the intervention was the first coordinated US-Japan action on the yen since June 1998, and the fix for Japan's Treasury problem is not the currency leg at all. Bessent has publicly proposed the Fed expand the FIMA repo facility, with Treasury willing to raise the cap, so Japan can borrow dollars against its Treasury holdings rather than sell them.

Visser's read on that is the honest one. FIMA is not money printing, and it is "a verbal bazooka indicating they are scared." Watch what it produced: the largest monthly rise in the US 30-year yield since this administration took over, and the highest monthly yield close in more than twenty years.

One caution on the source. Visser describes this as a dollar-yen operation throughout and never mentions the euro leg, and he lists no conditions attached to the rescue. This desk has been carrying both. Treat his account as filling in the mechanism rather than as agreeing on the terms.

4. Gold is beating positive real rates, and the household is paying the bill. Lyn Alden's framing, carried in the same Milk Road letter, is that gold rallying against positive real rates is supposed to be impossible. Fiscal dominance is what makes it possible: with debt above 100 percent of GDP, raising rates blows out the federal deficit faster than it slows bank lending. The policy rate stopped being a brake and became a line item.

The cost of that shows up in one series. Per the Financial Markets list and the St. Louis Fed, the 30-year mortgage is 6.69 percent, the highest since July 2025, with the 15-year at 6.01.

The decade on a median homeThenNow
30-year mortgage rate3.4 percent6.7 percent
Median price$250,000$446,000
Monthly payment$887$2,302, up 160 percent

The same letter carries a warning that private credit default rates are at recent highs and that internal loan-health reviews point to worse. That is the other end of the same rate: gold is the hedge against the deficit, and the mortgage and the private loan book are where the deficit gets paid for. Wednesday's print decides which of the two the Fed is allowed to care about.

item.title: The September hike was born on Tuesday and died on Friday
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Kashkari wanted it immediately, Warsh attached a condition, a negative payroll print destroyed the premise, and Bank of America still wants three hikes starting next month.
item.content:encoded:
Kashkari wanted it immediately, Warsh attached a condition, a negative payroll print destroyed the premise, and Bank of America still wants three hikes starting next month.

In five sessions this channel moved its own September call three times. That is either a system with no spine or a week in which the underlying facts genuinely reversed twice. It was the second one, and the reason is worth an entire memo, because the same sequence is about to repeat on Wednesday.

The chronology, because the order is the argument

DayWhat changed
TuesdayISM at 55.6, the best since May 2022, GDPNow raised to 6.2 percent
WednesdayKashkari says the Fed should begin raising now, backing 25 basis points
ThursdayThe Financial Times reports Warsh is prepared to raise in September, Cook says she is ready, Kalshi prices a hike this year at 65 percent
FridayPayrolls print minus 23,000 against plus 80,000, with May and June revised down 103,000
SaturdayBofA keeps 75 basis points starting September. Morgan Stanley says none this year

Three days of hawkish escalation, one data release, and a 75 basis point disagreement between two of the largest desks on the street. Nothing about the reaction function changed. What changed is that one side is weighting a survey and the other is weighting a payroll.

1. Warsh's condition has two legs, and the second one is a mirror

The Chair did not say he would hike. Per the Market list, he said he is prepared to raise rates in September if inflation prints run hot and markets price in higher borrowing costs.

Read the second clause again. The market pricing a hike is itself part of the trigger for one. That is a reaction function with a feedback loop inside it, and it means positioning is not merely predicting the decision, it is an input to it. When Kalshi went to 65 percent on Thursday, that number was not just a forecast. It was evidence toward Warsh's own condition.

Which is why Friday mattered more than it should have. Hike odds fell from 60 percent to 30 inside a morning. That did not only reprice the probability, it removed one of the two legs the Chair named.

The context underneath is the part nobody enjoys. The Wall Street Journal reported Trump held multiple undisclosed calls with Warsh, dated by Bloomberg to May. A Chair turning hawkish while taking private calls from a President who wants cheap money is the least comfortable possible sequence. It also argues the hawkishness is genuine, because political pressure runs the other way.

2. What the payroll print actually broke

Per the Polymarket list, the headline was minus 23,000 against an expected gain of 80,000. The revisions were worse: May and June cut by a combined 103,000.

A single negative month is noise. A negative month plus 103,000 taken off the two before it is a trend being discovered late, and it means the Fed spent three weeks arguing about tightening into a labour market that was already softer than the data on its desk.

The rest of the release complicates it rather than settling it.

July jobs reportReading
Unemployment4.1 percent, a one-year low
Average hourly earnings3.2 percent, slowing
Participation61.4 percent, down and near a five-year low
June JOLTS openingsdown 178,000 to 7.359 million against 7.454 expected

Unemployment falling to a one-year low in the same release that shows job losses is not a contradiction. It is what happens when people leave the labour force rather than lose jobs, and the St Louis Fed flagged prime-age participation as the line to read in this exact report before it landed.

So the hawkish case did not lose an argument. It lost its premise. You cannot run "the labour market is too tight" as a reason to hike when payrolls are negative and participation is falling.

3. Who is on each side, and the honest read of the gap

Per the August 7 Market list, Bank of America kept 75 basis points of hikes this year starting in September, explicitly after the print, on the stated reason that inflation remains the Fed's primary concern. Morgan Stanley's chief strategist says there will be no rate hikes this year.

That is the widest spread this channel has recorded between two large desks. Both cannot be roughly right.

Per the Polymarket list, Goldman supplied the frame that decides it: inflation now matters more than jobs for the Fed. If that is the reaction function, a cracking labour market is background rather than a reason to hold, and Wednesday's CPI is the whole question. The market has not fully picked a side either, with a 44 percent September hike still priced and more than one tightening built in before year end.

The dissent that deserves more weight than it gets is Invesco's, arguing the Fed is not behind the curve at all, with neutral at 3.5 to 4.0 percent against a current 3.50 to 3.75 range. If that is right, both the hikers and the cutters are solving a problem that does not exist.

4. The thing this week actually settled, which was not the Fed

While the rate argument went in circles, the funding story underneath it resolved. Joseph Wang, on the Financial Markets list: "Treasury has now spent all the ammo in their Exchange Stabilization Fund. They sold Euros to buy Yen because that's all they have in the ESF."

That confirmed something this channel had been calling a novel mechanism and reframed it as something worse. It was never a clever cross-currency strategy. Treasury sold euros because euros were what remained. Jordi Visser dates the action as the first coordinated US and Bank of Japan intervention since 1998, against 30-year yields at 20-year highs.

An empty stabilisation fund means the next yen defence needs either a Bank of Japan hike or Japan selling from its trillion dollars of Treasuries. Japan's own choice, as put plainly this week: raise rates and blow up the domestic debt market, or cut and kill the currency. There is no exit, only a decision about how it gets wrecked.

Set that beside Treasury guiding to $739 billion of privately held net marketable borrowing this quarter, $68 billion above the May estimate, with interest expense already running $827 billion through June against $749 billion a year earlier and 33 percent of the debt maturing inside twelve months. A September hike is not a 2027 problem for the fiscal path. It is a 2026 one.

What settles it, and what would change my mind

Wednesday, August 12, CPI. This is the print Warsh named. A hot core reading restores the first leg of his condition and Bank of America is right with a labour market cracking underneath. A soft one kills September and probably the year.

Tuesday, September 16, the FOMC. Between now and then the only other thing that matters is whether the payroll revisions continue, because two consecutive months of downward revisions stop being a data artifact and start being a recession signal.

I am at 65/35 for a September hold, above where this call started the week. I am less comfortable at 65 than the number suggests, for one reason: Bank of America is not a fringe desk, it looked at the same jobs report I did, and it did not blink. What would move me back toward a hike is a core CPI print above expectations combined with the market re-pricing the odds itself, because that combination satisfies both of Warsh's legs at once and he has told us in advance that it would.

What would move me further toward a hold is a third consecutive month of downward payroll revisions. That would make Friday a trend rather than an event, and no committee tightens into that.

The scoreboard, Macro & Policy

Ten calls settled on this channel's book. Read the raw number with care, because four of them are the same CLARITY event counted across four editions, so ten settled entries represent roughly six distinct events.

Resolved this week and lastOutcome
No CLARITY floor vote before the recess, house, 85/15Hit. Cloture never filed, Senate left, earliest procedural vote September 15
A Hormuz agreement inside two weeks, house, 60/40Hit. Iran and Oman agreed the route in two days, through Oman rather than the Qatari channel I named
Oil higher two weeks out, house, 65/35Miss. Called early and marked early. The route agreement removed the premium and I resolved it rather than letting the date lapse
Warsh and Bessent coordinating the buildout as a national project, Capital FlowsHit
The US intervening in the yen using euros, Prof G MarketsHit, and upgraded by Joseph Wang's confirmation that the fund is empty
Payrolls stronger but not a blowout, Kathy LienMiss by 103,000
Steil optimistic the Senate gets CLARITY across, relayedMiss
Kalshi and Polymarket odds moving up on CLARITY, relayedMiss. The direction reversed to an all-time low of 16 percent
Senate floor math rules out passage before recess, Brendan PedersenHit
CLARITY comes down to three or four Democrats, Josh RymanExpired. Never tested, no roll call happened

House record: 2 hits and 1 miss on three settled calls. That is a small enough sample that the percentage would be advertising rather than scorekeeping, so here is the number without the decoration: two right, one wrong, and the wrong one was an oil call I marked as a loss four days before its due date rather than waiting for the calendar to do it quietly.

Sixty-one open calls carried into next week. The ones that matter: the September hold at 65/35, revised twice in three days and now above where it started. CPI on Wednesday. A joint Iran-Oman announcement at 70/30, due Tuesday. Two Abqaiq calls due Friday. CLARITY not becoming law in 2026 at 85/15, raised from 80/20. The China AI dumping thesis. Japan's no-exit. And the Exchange Stabilization Fund being empty. That is the one I would least like to be wrong about, because it has no natural resolution date and the way you find out is a disorderly one.

item.title: Two independent desks put September near a coin flip, and I was at 35
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Benjamin Cowen has the hike at 43.9 percent and Jordi Visser at 45, the national debt crossed $40 trillion, and Iran hardened its terms for reopening the strait.
item.content:encoded:
Benjamin Cowen has the hike at 43.9 percent and Jordi Visser at 45, the national debt crossed $40 trillion, and Iran hardened its terms for reopening the strait.

This morning's memo said Wednesday's CPI settles September. It does. What changed over the weekend is that two people who model this for a living both put the hike near a coin flip, and my number was the most dovish on the board.

The week ahead. CPI lands Wednesday. Everything else is positioning into it.

September hike, as pricedReading
Benjamin Cowen43.9 percent
Jordi Visser45 percent
The Order Book, post-payrollsabout 40 percent, down from roughly 55
Kyle Reidhead35 percent, framed as "65 percent now agreeing with me"

Gold had the week the debasement trade wanted: up 7.2 percent, its third biggest week in 16 years, closing back above its 50-day for the first time since March after the third longest stretch below on record. Oil went the other way, near $75 and softening. The 30-year Treasury yield sits at a 19-year high.

1. I am trimming the hold call, and the reason is the distribution rather than the data. My 65/35 for a September hold implies a 35 percent hike. Per Benjamin Cowen that number is 43.9, and per Jordi Visser it is 45. The Order Book has the market at roughly 40 after the payroll print, down from 55 before it.

So three independent readings cluster between 40 and 45, and I was sitting outside them on the dovish side. I am moving to 60/40 for a hold. Not because the labour data changed over a weekend, but because being the most dovish voice on the board is a position that needs evidence I do not have.

Cowen supplies the mechanism I had underweighted. The two-year yield now sits above the 3.75 percent fed funds rate, and the Fed has historically chased the two-year rather than led it. His precedent is the late 1990s, where that chase ran for years before the cycle turned. A committee that is behind its own front end does not need a hot print to move. It needs an excuse.

2. Cowen's labour read is more careful than the headline and it argues against a recession. The July print was negative. His trigger is not that.

What Cowen actually watchesReading
Year-over-year total nonfarm payrollsnot negative. Every negative reading has been a recession. Came close in February and bounced
Initial claims189,000, roughly a 50-year low. His rule is that below 300,000 means no recession
Participation62.5 percent last November to 61.4 percent now
Unemploymentfell from 4.5 percent to 4.1, on participation rather than on hiring
His recession dashboard0.16, low

The growth rate is the honest worry. Total nonfarm grew 4 to 5 percent a year in 2022 and runs near 2 percent now, which he calls basically no net job creation. Visser's version is harder: aggregate weekly payrolls are at their weakest six-month rate of change since 2012 excluding the pandemic, average hourly earnings are down to 3.2 percent, and only healthcare has added jobs in 18 months.

Cowen's dated call is the one to carry, and it is about equities rather than the Fed. He expects a correction to begin by late September at the latest, keyed to midterm years 2014, 2018 and 2022, with the September 16 meeting as the pivot. That is falsifiable and it is six weeks out.

3. The debt crossed $40 trillion and the long end has stopped pretending. Per the August 8 Kalshi list, the number went through $40 trillion this week, roughly twice China's entire GDP, after adding $450 billion since July 1, over $15 billion a day. Kalshi prices $50 trillion by 2028 at 32 percent.

Per the Financial Markets list, Peter Mallouk put the consequence in one sentence: "You can't borrow trillions every year, tolerate persistently high inflation, and expect cheap financing forever." The 30-year at a 19-year high is that sentence with a price on it.

Two second-order items landed alongside it. Jan van Eck of VanEck says that by 2032 the government will not have enough to pay full Social Security benefits and scheduled payments drop 20 percent, "essentially a default in everything but name." And Japan's four largest life insurers now carry ¥15.13 trillion, about $96 billion, of unrealised domestic bond losses, up 7 percent in the quarter. That is the balance-sheet damage sitting behind the yen problem this channel has been tracking all week.

Anas Alhajji added the detail that reframes the intervention. Per the Nikkei read he cites, reopening Hormuz was one of five strings attached to the Bessent yen rescue, and joining in euros rather than dollars specifically reduced the pressure on Japan to liquidate Treasuries, which would have pushed the long end higher still.

4. Iran hardened its terms, and the reopening trade is now worse than it looked. Per the Kalshi list, Iran says the Strait of Hormuz "will not" return to its previous state. Per the Polymarket list, the price of reopening is now US forces withdrawn from the region, the naval blockade lifted, sanctions removed and frozen assets released.

Against that, Trump is reportedly willing to walk away from the conflict without a nuclear deal if the strait fully reopens. So both sides have moved toward a transaction and away from a settlement, and the transaction is expensive.

My 70/30 that a joint Iran-Oman announcement lands inside a week runs to Wednesday and it is now the call I am least comfortable with. A government listing four preconditions on Sunday is not a government signing on Wednesday. I am not revising it before the date because the route agreement itself is real and Oman is still the channel, but the honest read is that this resolves as a miss more often than 30 percent of the time from here.

The physical market has stopped caring either way. Anas Alhajji's second-quarter Asian demand data is negative across every country he tracks.

Q2 oil demand, year over yearChange
Chinaminus 12.0 percent
Pakistanminus 18.2 percent
Bangladeshminus 14.5 percent
Japanminus 6.2 percent
South Koreaminus 5.8 percent

Mike McGlone's conclusion follows from it: the North American liquids surplus is approaching 8 million barrels a day against near 3 million when WTI peaked near $130 in 2022, and "$40 crude is becoming normal." A closed strait was supposed to be the thing that broke that. It has not, and the demand side is why.

item.title: Two banks read the same payroll print and landed 75 basis points apart
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Bank of America still wants three hikes starting in September, Morgan Stanley says none this year, and Wednesday's CPI decides which desk was reading the right number.
item.content:encoded:
Bank of America still wants three hikes starting in September, Morgan Stanley says none this year, and Wednesday's CPI decides which desk was reading the right number.

Yesterday a negative payroll print killed the September hike in a morning. It did not kill the argument. Bank of America read the same number and kept three hikes.

The week ahead. Wednesday's CPI is the only print that matters, because it is the one Warsh named as his trigger. Friday's labour data set the table.

July jobs reportReading
Nonfarm payrollsminus 23,000 against plus 80,000 expected
May and June revisionsdown a combined 103,000
Unemployment4.1 percent
Average hourly earnings3.2 percent, slowing
Labour force participation61.4 percent, down slightly

Rate-hike probabilities fell roughly 20 points on the day. Gold took the week, finishing almost 8 percent higher, its biggest weekly gain since January per the Financial Markets list and more than the Nasdaq and S&P tracking funds combined.

1. The desks are further apart after the print than they were before it. Per the August 7 Market list, Bank of America stuck with 75 basis points of hikes this year starting in September, explicitly after payrolls fell 23,000 with 103,000 of downward revisions. Its stated reason is that inflation remains the Fed's primary concern.

Against that, per the Polymarket list, Morgan Stanley's chief strategist declared there will be "no rate hikes" this year.

That is a 75 basis point gap on the same data, the widest this product has recorded between two large desks all year. Both cannot be roughly right.

Goldman supplied the frame that decides it: inflation now matters more than jobs for the Fed. If that is the reaction function, then a labour market cracking is not a reason to hold, it is background, and Wednesday's CPI is the entire question. The market has not fully picked a side either. Per Anthony Pompliano's guest Jordi Visser, there is still a 44 percent chance of a September hike priced, with more than one tightening built in before year end.

My lean stays where I moved it Friday. 65/35 for a September hold. The reason is not the labour data, it is that Warsh named a conditional and the condition has to be met by a print rather than by an argument. But I am less comfortable at 65 than I was, because Bank of America is not a fringe desk and it looked at the same jobs report I did and did not blink.

2. China is dumping AI the way it dumped steel, and one of the analogies is worse than the other. Per Prof G Markets, tokens consumed from Chinese large language models went from 8 percent share in January 2025 to somewhere above 50 percent now. The framing offered is deliberate: China is "trying to do to our market what they tried to do to our steel market 30 or 40 years ago and doing in kind of 20 weeks to Silicon Valley what Japan did to Detroit over 20 years."

Twenty weeks against twenty years is the part to sit with. Trade dumping normally gives the incumbent time to lobby for tariffs. This did not.

The pricing evidence underneath is specific. Anthropic's cost to deliver what it charges $6,000 an hour for is not a software cost structure. Per the same show, the two American labs have already split on the response, with Anthropic going premium and OpenAI going for volume at lower cost, "and the Chinese are of course waiting on the sidelines to throw the story into complete turmoil."

The capex spread is the trade this creates. Everyone is spending $150 billion to $200 billion while Apple spends $11 billion, and the verdict offered is that this becomes a case study in whether it is better to wait out the uncertainty and then decide what factory to build, rather than build the factory first. This is the driver. What it does to the semis chain and to the names carrying the capex belongs to Stocks.

3. Japan has to pick how it gets wrecked, and the long end is already voting. Per Stocks with Josh, Japan holds over $1 trillion of US Treasuries, and the trap is that the Bank of Japan cannot sell enough of them to defend the yen without breaking the US bond market that funds American deficits. The choice as put: raise rates and blow up the domestic debt market, or cut and kill the currency. "There's no exit. They just simply have to pick how Japan gets wrecked."

This is the same thread that produced Thursday's confirmation that Treasury emptied its Exchange Stabilization Fund defending the yen, selling euros because euros were what remained. Visser adds the detail that dates it: this was the first coordinated US and Bank of Japan intervention since 1998, against 30-year yields at 20-year highs. His read is blunt. "The yen intervention is a representation that we have no more tools left."

The long end has already priced some of it. The main long-duration Treasury fund is pushing all-time lows since it launched in July 2002, yielding 5.14 percent, with a put-to-call skew near 7 to 1 and a short float around 20 percent. Per a widely-read breakdown, its historic drawdown dates read as a list of macro accidents, and the author adds the current one by name: 2007, 2013, 2018, 2020, 2023, 2025, and "August 2026, Kevin Warsh."

Being at an all-time low is not the same as being cheap. It is what a market looks like when it believes the supply and the policy both get worse. The position belongs to Stocks.

4. The Hormuz deal is close enough that the market has stopped paying for it. Per the August 7 Market list, Trump said the deal to reopen the strait is "moving along good" and stocks bounced on it. That is the seventh time this week he has said he wants an agreement. Bessent floated a ceasefire announcement over the weekend, and per the Polymarket list a US official set the condition plainly: the blockade of Iranian ports lifts once a deal restoring unimpeded commercial shipping is announced.

My 70/30 on a joint Iran-Oman announcement runs to Tuesday and is still live. What has changed is that the payoff has shrunk, because the tape now moves a few points on each headline instead of repricing crude.

The physical picture argues the same way. Global commercial crude inventories sit more than 40 million barrels higher than a year ago, and Anas Alhajji's read is the useful correction: the oil crisis is in petroleum products, not in crude. That is consistent with US pump prices setting a record $4.06 a gallon on August 4 while inventories build.

Two things sit against a clean resolution. ADNOC has logged 15 vessel attacks as the risk mounts, and Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed a defence agreement in Mecca on Friday. All three border Iran, and none of them signs that document if they expect the strait to be quietly settled next week.

So the week has one question and one date. If Wednesday's CPI runs hot, Bank of America is right and the September hike comes back with the labour market already cracking underneath it. If it does not, the hike is dead until the December meeting and everything above resolves toward the doves.

item.title: Payrolls lost 23,000 jobs and the September hike died in a morning
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: May and June were revised down a combined 103,000, Kalshi's hike odds fell from 60 percent to 30, and the S&P printed a record high on the news.
item.content:encoded:
May and June were revised down a combined 103,000, Kalshi's hike odds fell from 60 percent to 30, and the S&P printed a record high on the news.

Yesterday I reversed and said the Fed leans toward hiking in September. This morning's print took eighteen hours to make that look silly.

Market context. Per the Polymarket list, July nonfarm payrolls shed 23,000 jobs against expectations for an 80,000 gain, and May and June were revised down by a combined 103,000. The revisions are the worse half.

Where the rate path wentBeforeAfter
Kalshi, a hike this year60 percent30 percent, then 50 by the afternoon
Kalshi, Fed holds in Septembera 25bp hike was favourite67 percent, settling at 65
CME, a September hike54 percent on Thursdaythe print reversed it

Per the Kalshi list, unemployment hit a one-year low even as the payroll line went negative, and traders had been forecasting 4.2 percent. The S&P printed a new all-time high of 7,740 ninety minutes after the number. Gold futures went the other way and cleared $4,400, up 8.1 percent in 72 hours. CPI on August 12 is still the print Warsh named.

The scoreboard.

  • Wrong inside eighteen hours, and I am reverting. Yesterday I moved to 45/55 against a September hold on the strength of Warsh, Cook and Kashkari all turning hawkish in two days. A negative payroll print outranks three speeches. Back to 65/35 for a hold, above where I started.
  • Confirmed, and by the plumbing itself. I said Washington was defending the yen with euros. Joseph Wang, on the Financial Markets list: "Treasury has now spent all the ammo in their Exchange Stabilization Fund. They sold Euros to buy Yen because that's all they have in the ESF."
  • Resolved. Payrolls were the catalyst I flagged for today. Kathy Lien's "stronger payrolls, but probably not a blowout" missed by 103,000.
  • Due Wednesday. CPI, which now has to do all the work.

1. The revisions matter more than the headline, and the unemployment rate is lying. A single negative month is noise. A negative month plus 103,000 taken off the two before it is a trend being discovered late. That is the shape of a labour market that was already softer than the data said while the Fed was arguing about tightening into it.

The unemployment rate falling to a one-year low in the same release looks like a contradiction and is not. It is what happens when people leave the labour force rather than lose jobs. Per the Financial Markets list, the St Louis Fed flagged prime-age participation as the line to read in this exact report, noting more than half of the recent decline came from a January population correction and from ageing rather than from workers quitting.

June JOLTS pointed the same way before anyone was watching: openings down 178,000 to 7.359 million against 7.454 million expected, with the openings-to-unemployed ratio at 1.04.

So the hawkish case did not lose an argument. It lost its premise.

2. The Exchange Stabilization Fund is empty, and that closes the yen story. Joseph Wang's line above is the confirmation the euro-intervention story needed, and it reframes the whole thing. This was never a clever cross-currency strategy. Treasury sold euros because euros were what remained in the account.

An empty stabilisation fund means the next yen defence needs either the Bank of Japan raising rates or Japan selling reserves. Japan holds over a trillion dollars of Treasuries. Per the Crypto list, the ten-year sat at 4.73 percent with Fidelity's Jurrien Timmer calling anything above 4.5 percent the danger zone, and the warning attached is the one that matters: the Fed can cut and long yields can still rise.

Today's print pushes that day further out. It does not cancel it.

3. Bessent says he has Iran by the throat and the strait opens within days. Per the Polymarket list, the Treasury Secretary put a clock on it: "We have them by the throat, and they've got 150 to 180% food inflation, not able to pay the troops. I think shortly, maybe even today, tomorrow, we are going to see an agreement, a 30- to 60-day ceasefire, and the Strait will be open."

The enforcement numbers behind that leverage are real. Per the August 6 Polymarket list, CENTCOM has redirected 49 commercial vessels, disabled two and boarded two, and US imports of Saudi crude fell to zero in July, the first full month since 1985. Polymarket prices the blockade being lifted this month at 69 percent.

Tehran is not behaving like a government about to sign. An Iranian lawmaker has a preliminary bill barring US, Israeli and other hostile vessels from the strait with fines up to 20 percent of cargo value, and Trump's own read was "it's sort of open right now" with the caveat that "they can always shoot something."

Gold going up 8.1 percent in three days while a ceasefire is being announced tells you which one the money believes. I am 60/40 that a ceasefire is announced inside two weeks and under 50/50 that shipping volumes recover inside a month.

4. CLARITY is a September problem, and nobody filed the paperwork in time. Per the Financial Markets list, the Senate pushed the vote past summer recess. The mechanism was the one I named on Thursday: cloture was never filed. Eleanor Terrett had it live at the deadline, reporting worry on both sides that a failed cloture vote would bring the whole year-long effort down, and that if it was not filed that night it would not happen.

Elizabeth Warren supplied the durable objection, saying she supports crypto legislation but not this one, "written by the crypto industry to protect and advance the crypto industry." Thune ran out of floor time. Schumer wanted more talks.

Kalshi's odds it becomes law this year hit 16 percent, an all-time low. My 80/20 that it does not pass in 2026 is intact and I am raising it to 85/15, because the September calendar is already spoken for. The Senate comes back on the 14th with a government to fund and a Fed meeting two days later. Haseeb Qureshi is the useful counterweight, pointing out Kalshi still prices 30 percent plus for next year and above 50 percent by 2028. This bill is late, not dead, and the difference matters for anyone sizing a position on it.

item.title: Warsh opened the door to a September hike, and Trump has been calling him
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The Chair says he will raise if inflation runs hot, Kalshi prices a hike this year at 65 percent, and Treasury needs $739 billion of fresh borrowing in the same quarter.
item.content:encoded:
The Chair says he will raise if inflation runs hot, Kalshi prices a hike this year at 65 percent, and Treasury needs $739 billion of fresh borrowing in the same quarter.

Yesterday the hawk was a regional president nobody has to obey. Today it is the Chair, and the man who appointed him has been on the phone since May.

Market context. Per the Market list, the Financial Times reports Kevin Warsh is prepared to raise rates in September if inflation prints run hot and markets price in higher borrowing costs. The data underneath him came in firm.

Today's printsReading
Initial jobless claims199,000 against 204,000 expected
Continuing claimsup 24,000 to 1,801,000
Q2 productivity, preliminaryup 1.4 percent against 0.6 expected
Kalshi, a hike at some point this year65 percent

The dollar has not caught up to any of it. MUFG has the dollar index near a seven-week low and still undervalued against eight of the nine other G10 currencies, and Brent came back under $80. Payrolls land tomorrow. CPI on August 12 is the print Warsh named.

The scoreboard.

  • Wrong, and I am reversing it rather than defending it. Yesterday I went 55/45 that September is a hold. The Chair, Governor Lisa Cook and Neel Kashkari all turned hawkish inside 48 hours. I am now 45/55 against a hold.
  • Right, and nearly settled. On Monday I went 85/15 that no CLARITY floor vote happens before the recess. Kalshi prices that at 3 percent.
  • Working, and not the way the tape reads it. My 70/30 on a joint Iran-Oman announcement runs to August 12, and both governments are preparing to designate the strait a transit corridor. Ryan Petersen of Flexport counts one or two transits a day against almost 100 at the peak, at 10 to 15 percent war-risk insurance. The paper is nearly signed and the water is empty.
  • Due tomorrow. Payrolls, which decides whether Warsh's condition is met.

1. Warsh's condition has two legs, and the second one is a mirror. Per the Market list, people close to Warsh say he has acknowledged "early communication mistakes that blurred his message on price stability and Fed reform."

He named two triggers. Hot inflation prints, and markets pricing in higher borrowing costs. The second is the market itself, so a market that prices a hike is helping satisfy the condition for one.

The rest of the committee arrived in the same week. Per the Kalshi list, Governor Lisa Cook said she is ready to raise if inflation stays high and Kashkari said it is "slowly" time to raise. Invesco is the lone dissent that matters, and it argues about whether policy is already restrictive rather than about direction.

Then the part that is not economics. Per the Financial Markets list, the Wall Street Journal reports Trump held multiple undisclosed calls with Warsh, and Bloomberg dates them to May. A Chair turning hawkish while taking private calls from a President who wants cheap money is the least comfortable sequence available, and it argues the hawkishness is real.

2. Treasury needs $739 billion this quarter and the interest line already passed defense. Per ClearValue Tax, the August 3 Treasury statement guides to $739 billion of privately held net marketable borrowing for July through September, meaning debt sold to real buyers rather than shuffled between government accounts. That is $68 billion above the May estimate on less cash flow than projected. October through December is guided at $628 billion, $1.36 trillion across the back half.

The stock and its costFigure
Total debt$39.7 trillion
Interest expense through June$827 billion, against $749 billion a year earlier
Average rate on the debt3.36 percent in FY2025, about 3.42 percent now
Maturing inside twelve months33 percent

That last row is where sections one and two meet. A third of the stock reprices inside a year, so a September hike is not a 2027 problem for the fiscal path. It is a 2026 one. Lyn Alden, on the Stocks list, puts it blunter: for a reserve currency adding $2 trillion a year, the exit is debasement rather than default.

3. Washington is defending the yen with euros, and nobody has seen that before. Per Prof G Markets, the US is intervening in the yen market using euros, and their guest is unambiguous about how unusual that is: "I have never heard of any country intervening in anyone else's market using a third party currency before."

The mechanism is mundane. The US reserve pot is held predominantly in euros and yen, so euros are what there is to sell. The consequence is not. "The US authorities have been in touch with the European Central Bank," and selling euros in size against the yen puts the distortion in a third currency belonging to a central bank that did not ask for any of this.

The failure underneath explains why it got this exotic. Per Trader Mayne, Japan has spent $160 billion this year, including $53 billion and $34 billion on consecutive days last week, and the yen firms for a few days and then goes right back down. His conclusion is that reserves cannot fix it and only rate hikes can. Handle his next step carefully, because he sources it to an AI explainer rather than a report: a forced Bank of Japan hike unwinds the yen carry trade (borrowing cheap yen to buy higher-yielding assets abroad), and Japan sells Treasuries into it.

I am not putting odds on that chain. The near end carries enough. Two sources now describe the US financing a foreign currency defense while its own Chair talks about tightening, and MUFG names that intervention as a reason the dollar sits at a seven-week low. The softness is partly a policy choice executed in somebody else's money.

4. CLARITY needs 60 votes, has 53, and nobody filed the paperwork. Per Milk Road, the bill cleared the House 294 to 134 last July and Senate Banking 15 to 9 in May. On the floor it needs 60. Republicans hold 53.

The mechanics killed it before the politics got a turn. Per VirtualBacon, cloture (the motion that ends debate and forces a vote) had to be filed today to ripen in time for a Friday vote, and Majority Leader John Thune filed cloture on a different motion instead. Punchbowl reports Democrats settled on voting no as a bloc unless Republicans move on ethics, illicit finance and stablecoin yield.

The pricing followed the paperwork.

CLARITYNowBefore
Kalshi, passes before recess3 percent20 percent yesterday
Kalshi, becomes law this year20 percent, an all-time low25 percent on Wednesday
Polymarket, becomes law in 202615 to 17 percent50 to 70 percent in January

Friday is the last scheduled working day. Senator Cynthia Lummis says the Senate sits into the weekend with recess starting Monday, the only reason this is not finished already. Per the People to follow list, LuxAlgo answered the countdown with "News flash: It ain't happening."

Here is the calendar that replaces it. The Senate returns September 14 into a handful of working days and a government to fund, against a Fed meeting Warsh has just made live. A committee arguing about a hike does not clear floor time for market-structure legislation, and 20 percent for the whole year says the market has worked that out.

item.title: Iran and Oman agreed the Hormuz route, and gold rose four percent anyway
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: The strait is being reopened by the mediator nobody named, Kashkari wants a hike immediately, and the Street is now split six ways on September with Kalshi at a coin flip.
item.content:encoded:
The strait is being reopened by the mediator nobody named, Kashkari wants a hike immediately, and the Street is now split six ways on September with Kalshi at a coin flip.

Yesterday Bessent said a Hormuz deal might land today or tomorrow and pointed at Qatari draft text. The deal is landing. The mediator turned out to be Oman, and gold is behaving as though none of it happened.

Market context. Per the Market list, Iran's foreign ministry confirmed three things in the space of two minutes: the geographic characteristics of the route through the Strait of Hormuz have been agreed by Iran and Oman, a joint announcement is in its final stage if "certain third parties" do not interfere, and the agreement "in itself" does not mean the strait is secure.

The rates picture moved further than the geopolitics did.

Where September sitsReading
Kalshi, hold49 percent
Kalshi, 25bp hike47 percent
Kalshi, more than 25bp2 percent
ISM Manufacturing55.6, seventh straight month of expansion
S&P 500 net profit margin16.7 percent, a FactSet record since 2009
Gold futuresup 4 percent on the day, above $4,300

Payrolls land Friday against a 91,000 to 120,000 consensus, and CPI follows on August 12.

The scoreboard.

  • Working, and through the wrong door. I went 60/40 yesterday that a Hormuz agreement gets announced inside two weeks. The route is agreed and a joint announcement is in its final stage. I had the channel wrong, because Qatar's draft text was not the one that closed it.
  • Miss, and I am calling it now rather than waiting for the date. On August 2 I went 65/35 that oil would be higher two weeks out. Three sessions later there is a signed route and the risk premium is gone. The call runs to August 16 and it is not coming back.
  • Due Friday. Payrolls, which everything this week routes through.

1. Oman closed it, and the hedge in Iran's own statement is the part to read. The sequence matters because it tells you who actually has leverage. Bessent named Qatar yesterday and put a 24-hour clock on it. What arrived instead was an Iran-Oman route agreement, with Tehran adding two qualifications in the same breath.

The first is procedural: the joint announcement happens if "certain third parties" do not interfere. That is a pre-built escape hatch, and it is aimed at Washington and Jerusalem.

The second is substantive and more important. An agreed route is not a secure strait. Iran is conceding transit geography while explicitly reserving the right to treat passage as conditional. That is the same permissioned-corridor structure it described on Sunday, now with a signature attached.

So the reopening is real and the de-risking is partial. Per the Market list, Russia hit three cargo vessels in the Black Sea the same day. Shipping risk is not a single-theatre story.

I am 70/30 that a joint announcement is made inside a week, up from 60/40 on the route agreement. The 30 is the third-party clause, and the reason I am not higher is that Iran has now written its own permission to walk away into the text.

2. Kashkari wants a hike now, and the Street cannot agree on anything. Per the Market list, Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari said the Fed should begin raising rates now, backing 25 basis points and warning that delay could force more aggressive tightening if inflation becomes entrenched. He was one of the three who dissented last week.

Then look at how far apart the desks are on the same meeting.

DeskSeptember and beyond
BofA25bp in September, then October and December
JPMorganHold in September, hike in December
GoldmanHold, no more hikes
Morgan StanleyHold through year-end
BarclaysHold through year-end
CitiHold in September, then cuts in October, December and January

BofA's own chief executive Brian Moynihan reiterated the three-hike forecast publicly, saying the labour market is strong while inflation still needs to ease. Citi is at the opposite pole with three cuts. Those cannot both be roughly right.

Janet Yellen supplied the frame that fits the data best. The labour market is functioning well and no longer looks hot enough to fuel inflation, and she is surprised the Middle East conflict and higher oil prices have had such limited economic impact. Her conclusion is that the challenge is still bringing inflation down without harming the economy.

My lean. I am 55/45 that September is a hold, down from the near-certainty of a month ago, and the reason is Kashkari rather than the data. Three dissents plus a regional president publicly campaigning for immediate action is how a committee talks itself into moving. The cleanest read is that the hike is a question of timing, not direction, and Citi's cut scenario requires something to break that has not broken.

3. Goldilocks arrived and the pipeline warning did not clear. Per Milk Road, the case is genuinely strong. ISM at 55.6 is the best since May 2022 and the seventh consecutive month of expansion. S&P 500 net profit margins hit 16.7 percent, the highest FactSet has recorded since it began tracking in 2009. And inflation cooled in the latest reading after several months of increases, partly because easing Iran tensions took energy prices down.

Growth accelerating while inflation falls is the setup that makes everything work, and it is why the equity tape looks the way it does.

Two things sit against it and both are dated. ISM Prices Paid is still at 71.1, elevated on tariff-driven input costs, and that has not passed through yet. And the breadth measure that held the same index at caution yesterday has not recovered.

Which is why Friday matters more than any of it. A payroll print inside consensus puts a labour market under the ISM surge and the Goldilocks read holds. A second consecutive miss near June's 57,000 leaves a strong manufacturing survey next to a weakening jobs market, and that combination has historically resolved toward the jobs data rather than the survey.

4. Gold is up four percent and is not supposed to be. Per the Crypto list, gold futures extended gains to 4 percent on the day and rose above $4,300 an ounce, with the metal running from roughly $370 to almost $392 on the tracking fund in two sessions.

Read that against everything above. The war premium is leaving oil, the strait is reopening, equities are at records and margins are the best since 2009. Gold should have nothing to do.

Instead it is the strongest thing on the board, which says the bid is not geopolitical. It is either the rate path, where a committee arguing about immediate hikes while a Treasury Secretary asks for a Fed facility to be enlarged is exactly the institutional picture gold responds to, or it is currency, with the same Treasury endorsing a stronger yen days after intervening to get one.

Mike McGlone's line is the useful counterweight and it belongs here: copper, gold and Bitcoin are all sock puppets to the S&P 500 right now. If he is right, gold is simply levered risk appetite and carries no signal at all. I lean against him at 60/40, because equities and gold have now risen together for two sessions while oil fell, and that combination is a monetary story rather than a risk-appetite one.

item.title: Bessent says a Hormuz deal may land tomorrow, and oil gave up two percent
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Qatar has draft text ready, futures hit a record high on the headline, and the same Treasury Secretary spent the morning telling the Federal Reserve to upsize one of its own facilities.
item.content:encoded:
Qatar has draft text ready, futures hit a record high on the headline, and the same Treasury Secretary spent the morning telling the Federal Reserve to upsize one of its own facilities.

Three days ago Iran was denying it had agreed to reopen the Strait of Hormuz while CENTCOM redirected 35 vessels around it. This morning the Treasury Secretary said a deal might be signed by tomorrow. Everything else on the board moved off that one sentence.

Market context. Per the Financial Markets list, Scott Bessent said "I think there's a chance we may have a deal today or tomorrow to open the strait," and Qatar has already prepared draft text for an agreement. Futures hit a record high on it. Oil rose 2 percent and then fell 2 percent inside the same session, with Brent for October at $81.50.

The domestic data was the quiet half and it was strong.

PrintReading
July ISM Manufacturing55.6 percent, best since May 2022
ISM Prices Paid71.1, still elevated on tariff-driven input costs
Atlanta Fed GDPNow, Q3raised from 5.0 to 6.2 percent
US trade balancenegative $73.3 billion against negative $73.0 expected, prior negative $77.6

Ahead: payrolls Friday August 7, consensus 91,000 to 120,000 after June's 57,000 miss, then CPI on August 12.

The scoreboard.

  • Hit, and it was mine to publish. I said yesterday the Camp David notepad reading "buy Japanese yen $5-10 bil" was deliberate rather than accidental. Confirmed from both sides. The New York Fed, acting for Treasury, sold euros to buy yen on Friday, both governments acknowledged it Monday, and USD/JPY fell from above 163 to around 156.
  • Against, for a second day. I went 65/35 on August 2 that oil would be higher two weeks out. Bessent is now negotiating the exact opposite. That call is losing and I am not going to dress it up.
  • Confirmed and dated. The CLARITY Act cleared the House and Senate Banking, sits on the legislative calendar, and still has no scheduled vote with the recess on Saturday.

1. The strait is being traded before it is open, and the draft text is the tell. Per the Financial Markets list, Anas Alhajji timed the tape precisely: oil rose 2 percent, then fell 2 percent once Bessent spoke. Per 0xResearch, Trump's decision to postpone further strikes against Iran had already sent Brent down 4.7 percent on Monday.

So the risk premium has come out in two steps on two statements, and neither of them is an open waterway. Qatar having draft text is the genuinely new fact, because a mediator does not circulate paper without a landing zone in view.

The cost of the closure is now measurable in fiscal terms. Alhajji counts EU governments committing roughly 12 to 16 billion euros in subsidies and measures to cushion the crisis and hold energy costs down. In most countries that spending prevented a recession, growth stayed very low anyway, and the borrowing still has to be repaid.

My lean, and it is a downgrade from Sunday. I am 60/40 that a Hormuz agreement is announced inside two weeks, up from roughly even, because Qatari draft text plus a US Treasury Secretary putting a date on it is a different state from either side making claims. The 40 is that Iran has denied three separate reopening reports in four days.

2. The Treasury Secretary spent the morning directing a Federal Reserve facility. This is the item almost nobody priced. Per the Crypto list, Bessent's statement on the yen ran past the intervention itself and into instrument design.

His words. "We will not hesitate to participate in further joint intervention. The FIMA Repo Facility is an important backstop. We would encourage it to be upsized in the coming months."

Jeff Park caught what that means and said it in one line: "FIMA is entirely a Fed tool, not a Treasury tool. Welcome to the Bessent-Warsh era of Fed interdependence."

He is right and it matters more than the yen level. The Foreign and International Monetary Authorities repo facility lets foreign central banks borrow dollars against their Treasury holdings rather than dumping them. It is the Fed's plumbing for stopping a forced sale of US paper. A Treasury Secretary publicly asking for it to be enlarged is fiscal authority making a monetary request in the open, and neither institution corrected the other.

Bessent also went further than a stabilisation argument, saying Treasury "strongly supports Japan's decisive market and monetary steps to correct the substantial undervaluation of the yen," and describing the Takaichi government as moving into a new phase of Abenomics. That is the United States endorsing a stronger yen, which tightens the cheapest funding pipe in global markets.

3. The economy printed strong and the index that watches it still says caution. Per Milk Road, July ISM at 55.6 percent answered the growth question in the clearest way available, GDPNow extended to 6.2 percent rather than retracing, and the stress score fell to its floor while the macro buffer sat at full strength. Oil held below $80, copper rose, freight costs fell and the curve steepened.

And their posture stayed at caution at 75 percent exposure, for one reason. Breadth on the market side fell 0.46 on the week to 0.18, working directly against every other gain, even as the equal-weight S&P keeps outrunning the cap-weighted index and the rotation carries into August. The rotation is visible in prices and absent from the breadth score, and that gap is the only thing between here and a full risk-on posture.

Their three conditions to clear it are worth writing down: breadth stops falling, Friday's payrolls confirm a labour market under the ISM surge, and the August 12 CPI leaves six-month core flat. That last one is the live risk, because ISM Prices Paid at 71.1 is a tariff-driven pipeline warning that has not bled through yet.

Mohamed El-Erian adds the distributional caveat on the Financial Markets list: more than 80 percent of reporters have beaten expectations, and releases like McDonald's this morning keep showing the K, with pressure concentrated on lower-income households.

4. CLARITY has four days and no floor time. Per Arbitrage Andy, the bill has cleared the House and advanced through Senate Banking, and it is formally on the Senate legislative calendar, meaning it is eligible for a floor vote. It has no scheduled vote and Congress leaves for recess on Saturday.

The arithmetic is the whole story. Cloture needs 60 votes, so roughly seven Democratic senators have to cross. Some backed earlier committee versions and negotiations have since stalled on three things: ethics provisions covering government officials' own crypto activity, consumer protection language, and stablecoin-related banking concerns.

Polymarket prices 27 percent that it is signed into law this year. That is the number to carry, and it is down from 82 percent in February.

The consequence if it lapses is not a price move, it is a jurisdictional vacuum. Without the bill the SEC and CFTC turf war stays unresolved and exchanges, token issuers and crypto businesses keep operating in legal limbo. I am 85/15 that no floor vote happens before the recess, and the more interesting question is whether September brings a rewrite or a shelving.
